# ON THE LAW OF WAR

<margin>Soto, Book 4, question 7, article 2. Covarruvias on the chapter *peccatum*, part 2, section 1. Silvester on the word *Restitutio* (Restitution), number 3, question 6.</margin>
Those rules which are commonly proposed by theologians who instruct the internal tribunal of the conscience.

III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held beyond the simple value of the thing based on his own actions) is not held to any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither does he have the thing itself, nor any gain from it.

<margin>Medina on contracts, question 10. Zeffi, Book 2, chapter 14. Navarrus, chapter 17, number 7.</margin>
IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is held to restore also the existing fruits of the thing: I say the fruits of the thing; for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have been produced without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is based on ownership. For he who is the owner of the thing is naturally the owner of the fruits of the thing.

V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the thing and consumed fruits, if he would have consumed just as much in any other way: for in this he is considered to have become wealthier. Thus, Caius Caesar Caligula <margin>Suetonius, chapter 16.</margin> is praised because, at the beginning of his reign, to those whom he restored to their kingdoms, he also added the fruits of the intermediate time.

VI. Fourth, he is not held for the fruits which he neglected to gather: because he has neither the thing, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor has given to another a thing donated to him, he is not held unless he would have donated just as much even without this thing: for then it will be a gain to have spared his own property.

<margin>Law: *Quivas*, final section, Digest on Theft.</margin>
VIII. Sixth, if he has sold a purchased thing, he is not held, unless perhaps he sold it for more: but if he sold a donated thing, he is held to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not otherwise have squandered.

<margin>Law: *Si & rem*, Digest on the petition of inheritance.</margin>
IX. Seventh, a thing belonging to another, bought in good faith, must be restored, nor can the price expended be reclaimed. To this rule, it seems to me that an exception must be added: unless the owner could not have recovered the possession of his own thing without some expenditure in a likely manner, for example, if the thing was in the hands of pirates. <margin>Law: *Sed & si lege*, Digest on the same. Law: *Si eum servum*, Digest on borrowed things. Law: *Mater tua*; Law: *Si mancipia*, Digest on the vindication of things.</margin> For then, it will be possible to deduct the amount the owner would have willingly spent. For the possession of the fact itself, especially when recovery is difficult, is something estimable, and in this, the owner is considered to have become wealthier after the loss of the thing. And therefore, although the purchase of his own thing is not valid by ordinary law, Paulus the Jurist nevertheless says it is valid if, from the beginning, it was agreed that the possession which is with another should be purchased. <margin>Law: *Sucr*, Digest on contracted purchase. Law 1, Digest on evictions.</margin> Nor do I require here that the thing be purchased with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say that an action for the management of affairs arises. <margin>Law: *Si laborav*, section *Si navis*, Digest on the Rhodian Law. Sylvester on the word *quid de praedam ementibus* (what of those buying from plunder). Aegidius Regius, distinction 35, doubt 7, number 126. Hostiensis, title on the law of war. a Law: *Si in emtione*, section *rei*, Digest on contracted purchase.</margin>

<summary>This page defines the obligations of a possessor in good faith regarding the restitution of property, including the treatment of fruits, consumed items, and expenses incurred during recovery.</summary>
<keywords>Good faith, restitution, ownership, fruits, Caius Caesar Caligula, Paulus the Jurist, pirates, contracts</keywords>
